title: In 10 dimensions, where are the points?
hook: Scatter points evenly in a box. Add dimensions. Does the middle stay crowded?

knows: random points scattered in a square
that a model can use many features
doesNotKnow: how space behaves in many dimensions
that almost every point sits near an edge once there are many dimensions

misconception: Adding more features only adds information; points spread evenly stay mostly in the middle and nearby points stay nearby.
objective: The learner can explain that a point only needs to be near an edge in one dimension, so in many dimensions almost every point is near an edge, and that this is why distances and 'nearest' behave strangely there.

claims.text: A point spread evenly in a cube is within 5% of a face in one dimension with chance 10%, so it avoids every edge in d dimensions with chance 0.9^d; the near-a-wall share is 1 − 0.9^d: 10% (1-D), 19% (2-D), 65.1% (10-D), 99.997% (100-D).
claims.source: Independence of coordinates of a uniform point in the unit cube; 0.9^10 = 0.3487. Reproduced by exactShare in Demo.tsx.

claims.text: In 500 seeded draws of 200 points in 10 dimensions, the near-a-wall count ranged from 108 to 149 (54% to 75%).
claims.source: spread(10, 500) in Demo.tsx, seeds 1-500 (seed*1000 + d into mulberry32), untuned. The stage's draws use seeds 1, 2, 3, ... in order, also untuned; draw 1 at 10-D gives 132 of 200.

claims.text: The 5% edge band is the toy's own convention, labelled on the stage.
claims.source: Chosen for the toy (brief 21 in company/domains/briefs/ai.md); a different band changes the numbers, not the trend.

claims.text: In many dimensions points end up far apart and distances concentrate, so 'nearest neighbour' stops meaning near.
claims.source: About real methods: Beyer, Goldstein, Ramakrishnan & Shaft 1999, 'When is nearest neighbor meaningful?' (ICDT); Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman 2009, The Elements of Statistical Learning, §2.5. · Fact-check 2026-10-13: Holds under the conditions of Beyer et al. (distance concentration); real data of low intrinsic dimension can behave better. The reveal states it as the toy lesson, acceptable.

recall.question: A model compares customers on 50 features, each scaled 0 to 1. Roughly how many customers look 'extreme' (near the top or bottom 5%) on at least one feature?
recall.why: A customer only needs to be extreme on one feature. Avoiding the edge on all 50 takes 0.9^50, about 0.5%, so nearly everyone is extreme somewhere.
